title: Prefetch routing & batching cost sandbox demo - Aquila Tech
summary: Short walkthrough of Redwood Optimize console focusing on prefetch routing, batch sizing, and KV/prefix cache settings. Demoed cost model simulator with Aquila's typical traffic profile and discussed pilot parameters (2-week sandbox + benchmark). Security and deployment questions surfaced (SOC2, SSO, KMS) — Redwood to share security pack and sandbox access. Agreed next step: run a 2-week pilot, Redwood to provision sandbox and cost spreadsheet.
topics: Dynamic batching and target latency SLOs
KV/prefix cache TTL and eviction strategies
Cost model simulation with Aquila traffic profile
action_items: Jamie Patel: Share cost-model spreadsheet and console sandbox link by 2027-11-10
Lena Ortiz: Prepare benchmark runbook and recommended batch/prefetch knobs by 2027-11-12
Alex Gomez: Provide 1 week of anonymized request traces (gzipped) for simulation by 2027-11-11
next_steps: Redwood to provision a 2-week sandbox with Optimize console presets for Aquila's profile
Customer to run Redwood's benchmark with infra lead + Redwood SE on call (schedule week of 2027-11-15)
Redwood to send SOC2 and KMS integration docs and draft pilot agreement
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-11-08 15:00 PST | Duration: 42 minutes | Attendees: Jamie (Redwood AE), Lena (SE), Theo (PM), Alex (CTO, Aquila), Maya (Infra), Priya (PM)

[00:00] Jamie (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jamie from Redwood, with Lena and Theo on the call. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Alex (Aquila CTO): Good, thanks. Were excited to see the Optimize console in action. We sent a note about prefetched routing and how it should behave under bursty traffic.
[00:15] Lena (Redwood SE): Great, we'll jump into the console. Quick agenda: show the prefetch/lookahead options, routing policies, and then the cost-simulator with your sample traffic assumptions.
[00:24] Maya (Aquila Infra): Quick FYI, security folks are watching for SOC2 and KMS integration — we may ask for compliance docs after the demo.
[00:31] Jamie: Totally expected, we'll share the security pack. Also thinking of a two-week sandbox so you can run real workloads.
[00:36] Theo (Optimize PM): I'll start by pulling up the Optimize dashboard. You can see here we have preset strategies: latency-first, cost-first, and balanced. I'm going to select balanced for demo.
[00:46] [00:46] Theo: The prefetch lookahead slider controls how many tokens/steps we warm in KV cache ahead of generation. For most dialog apps a 2-3 token lookahead gives good hit rates without overfetching.
[00:58] Priya (Aquila PM): Sorry, how does lookahead interact with session cache? We use session affinity to keep the KV cache sticky per user session.
[01:05] Lena: Good question. Prefetch is orthogonal to session cache: session cache keeps the user's full KV, while prefetching primes the prefix for common next-token patterns. If you have high session reuse, you benefit less from aggressive prefetching.
[01:20] Alex: Our product is a mixed-use chat with long histories — average request length is 120 tokens and many follow-on questions. Does that mean we should avoid high lookahead?
[01:29] Lena: Not necessarily. With long histories the KV size grows but hit rates for the immediate prefix can still be high. The tradeoff is memory and prefetch cost. In the cost-simulator I'll show the delta.
[01:40] [01:40] Theo: Switching to the routing tab — routing policy lets you split traffic across model variants and capacity tiers. For example, we can route 70% to a quantized cheaper model and 30% to a low-latency variant. You can express this as a hard percentage or set latency thresholds.
[01:56] Maya: Does routing support real-time fallback if a node is busy? We can't have requests queue for too long.
[02:02] Theo: Yes, there's an automatic fallback policy. If the selected variant's tail latency rises above the threshold, we route to the fallback variant in milliseconds. It's in the routing policy as "auto-fallback".
[02:12] [02:12] Jamie: I'm going to run the cost simulator with a representative profile you sent — 20k requests/day, 120 token avg, 4 concurrent users per second burst. Theo, can you walk through the knobs?
[02:23] Theo: Sure. First we choose concurrency target and allowed tail latency (p50/p95). Then batch window and max batch size. For cost-first we bias larger batch windows to increase token throughput; for latency-first we cap batch window to keep p95 low.
[02:36] Theo: I'm setting batch window to 25ms, max batch size to 64, prefetch lookahead 2 tokens, session cache TTL 6 hours, and KV eviction policy LRU.
[02:46] [02:46] Theo: Running simulation... this will compare per-token cost and expected p95 latency across three routing mixes: 100% low-cost model, 70/30 low/high, and 100% high-perf.
[02:58] Lena: While that runs, a quick aside on eviction: if your KV grows fast, set a per-session TTL plus a global cache size cap. That prevents disproportionate memory usage.
[03:10] Alex: We use dynamic conversations where users often come back after hours; TTL of 6 hours seems fine. How does cache warmup behave after a cold restart?
[03:18] Lena: Cold starts mean no KV; we recommend prefetch during session startup if the first prompt is deterministic. For non-deterministic prompts you get gradual warmup; routing policies can send first N requests to high-perf nodes to keep UX smooth during warmup.
[03:30] [03:30] Theo: Results ready: with your profile, the balanced routing mix shows a 42% cost reduction vs 100% high-perf while p95 latency stays under 220ms. If we go 100% low-cost, cost drops 60% but p95 jumps to ~420ms.
[03:46] Priya: Those numbers look promising. Is the simulator using our real CPU/GPU cost assumptions or Redwood defaults?
[03:52] Theo: Right now Redwood defaults; Jamie, Ill switch to Aquila's cost inputs.
[03:57] [03:57] Theo: Paste your VM/GPU unit prices... ok that's loaded. Re-running simulator... new results: balanced is a 35% savings and p95 ~240ms. 100% low-cost is 55% savings but p95 ~380ms.
[04:12] Maya: We also need to consider request-level SLAs — some customers want <150ms for certain flows. Can we mark routes as "high-priority" for those flows?
[04:20] Theo: Yes you can tag routes. In the console you can create route rules based on request metadata (customer tier, route path) and pin them to high-perf variants.
[04:29] [04:29] Jamie: I want to highlight KV prefetch cost: prefetch increases upstream token cost because it loads tokens into KV proactively. If hit rates are >60% the net per-session token cost often goes down because you avoid re-generating long prefixes. If hit rates are low, prefetch becomes waste.
[04:45] Alex: How do we estimate expected hit rate?
[04:48] Lena: We use historical traces to estimate prefix repetitiveness. Your logs will show common prompt starters, which are excellent prefetch targets. Also prefix length matters — 8-16 token prefixes capture many templated intros.
[05:00] [05:00] (sound of typing)
[05:04] Theo: I'm uploading a short example trace you sent earlier into the simulator, anonymized. Running a hit-rate analysis... Estimated prefix hit-rate: 62% for 8-token prefixes, 48% for 12-token.
[05:14] Priya: So 8-token lookahead looks sweet.
[05:16] Lena: Right, 8-token prefetch with session affinity + a 6-hour TTL is a common pattern for long-history chat.
[05:22] [05:22] Alex: What about memory pressure on the serving nodes — will prefetch bloat memory and cause OOMs?
[05:27] Lena: That's why we have per-pool memory caps and eviction policies. We can limit per-session KV size and total pool memory. If memory hits the cap, we evict least-recently-used sessions.
[05:37] [05:37] Maya: How is this different when you're on Redwood Dedicated vs Hosted API? We have compliance needs that push us to dedicated but we need throughput guarantees.
[05:45] Jamie: Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and stricter isolation; the runtime still supports the same prefetch and routing knobs. The main difference is predictability and SLA terms — dedicated is the right move if you need guaranteed throughput and data residency.
[05:58] Lena: Architecturally it's the same runtime; the console just points at your dedicated pool. Some hardware-specific kernel choices differ but the controls are identical.
[06:08] [06:08] Theo: Back to simulator — I'm toggling the batch window to 10ms to see latency-first behavior. Result: p95 drops to ~160ms but cost increases ~18% vs balanced.
[06:20] Priya: Is there an automatic optimizer that picks batch window for target p95?
[06:24] Theo: Yes, Optimize has an "auto-tune" mode where you set a latency target and budget constraint and it searches combinations of batch window and max-batch-size. It runs offline using traces to propose safe defaults.
[06:36] Alex: If we run the auto-tune on our traces how confident are we that the recommended knobs will generalize under spikes?
[06:42] Lena: We add a safety margin based on spike percentiles you choose. For example, pick the 99th percentile traffic spike and it will bias knobs to meet the p95 under that spike.
[06:52] [06:52] (background noise)
[06:55] Maya: About security: we need to confirm KMS integration and whether Redis on the cache plane is encrypted in transit.
[07:01] Jamie: We'll send the security pack with KMS and keystore details. For Dedicated we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. For Hosted we support Redwood-managed KMS with customer-managed keys (CMKs).
[07:12] Priya: Any gotchas for SSO/SAML?
[07:15] Lena: SSO is standard SAML/OIDC; sometimes the nameID mapping is a small config step. Our customer success team helps with it during pilot.
[07:24] [07:24] Alex: Ok, on pricing — curious if you can show a raw token-level cost breakdown.
[07:29] Theo: Yep, the simulator outputs per-token compute cost, memory amortized cost, and prefetch overhead. I'll export the sheet and drop a link in the notes.
[07:38] (pause)
[07:40] Theo: Link (short): bit.ly/redwood-aquila-cost-demo (demo-only data).
[07:45] Alex: Got it, we'll look.
[07:47] [07:47] Jamie: Quick point about billing: Hosted is usage-based per token; Dedicated is committed capacity plus overage. In Dedicated we usually present a recommended commit sized by your peak x buffer.
[07:59] Maya: For the pilot we'd prefer Hosted sandbox first then move to Dedicated if results look good.
[08:05] Jamie: That's a common path. We'll provision a hosted sandbox with dedicated quota to mimic dedicated behaviour.
[08:12] [08:12] Theo: There's also a "sandbox cost mode" where tokens are simulated without incurring customer bill — good for prototyping.
[08:20] Priya: Great. Can we also simulate a mixed routing where certain API keys always get high-perf?
[08:26] Theo: Absolutely — route by API key tag. You can pin keys to variants or tiers.
[08:31] [08:31] (crosstalk)
[08:33] Alex: A few operational questions: what telemetry do we get? We need per-route token breakdowns, per-token latency histograms, and kv-hit metrics.
[08:41] Lena: The console provides token-level costing, per-model latency histograms, KV hit/miss rates, and trace-based sampling for error analysis. You can export or hook to Datadog/NewRelic with tracing hooks.
[08:54] Maya: Do you keep raw logs? For compliance we may need audit logs retained for 12 months.
[08:59] Jamie: Retention is configurable, and for Dedicated we can support longer retention windows. We'll include retention SLAs in the pilot docs.
[09:10] [09:10] Theo: Im going to flip to a short scenario: take medium-tail traffic and add a sudden 5x burst for 30 seconds. Watching the simulator — with balanced routing, tail latency spikes to ~340ms then fallback triggers to high-perf variant and stabilizes. Cost increases but user-visible latency recovers.
[09:29] Alex: So fallback reduces user impact while increasing cost temporarily. That's acceptable if we keep it short.
[09:34] Lena: Exactly, and you can set budget caps to prevent runaway cost — if cost overrun exceeds threshold, we can throttle prefetch or temporarily reduce prefetch depth.
[09:44] [09:44] Priya: Are there any knobs specifically to reduce cold-start impact?
[09:47] Theo: Yes — pre-warm pools, keep warm VMs and replicate KV snapshots for hot sessions. There's also a warm-start route that sends first N requests to warm hosts.
[09:58] Alex: How much extra cost does warm pools add?
[10:02] Theo: Depends on the size; for your profile a single 8-GPU warm pool for hot routes would add ~8-12% to baseline cost but cut cold-start latency by ~60-70%.
[10:15] [10:15] (longer pause while screenshare)
[10:20] Lena: We've captured the console presets you'd likely use: batch-window 25ms, max-batch 64, prefetch 8 tokens for templated flows, session TTL 6h, routing balanced with 30% high-perf pin for critical routes.
[10:35] Alex: That seems sensible. One last thing: our procurement team will want a rough committed spend estimate for Dedicated. Can you provide a sizing recommendation?
[10:43] Jamie: We'll produce a sizing sheet from the simulator using your 99th percentile traffic and add a buffer — estimate and recommended commit will be included in the follow-up.
[10:53] Theo: Also note quantization options: a quantized 4-bit model can cut compute cost ~35% with minor accuracy differences. We can include a quick eval of quality delta if you want.
[11:06] Maya: Please include that.
[11:08] [11:08] Jamie: Ok, quick recap: Redwood will share sandbox link, cost spreadsheet, SOC2/KMS docs. Aquila will provide an anonymized trace and schedule the benchmark run. We'll aim to kick off the sandbox by 2027-11-15.
[11:23] Priya: Works for us.
[11:25] Alex: Thanks, this was helpful.
[11:27] Jamie: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the benchmark.
[11:33] (meeting ends)

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-heard terms (e.g., "K-V cash" vs KV cache) and brief overlaps. The speaker labels are mainly accurate but some timestamps may be off by a few seconds.
